titulo: How they talk when it isn't to you
subtitulo: Two people at a bar, at the speed they actually use it, and twelve of the sentences in there are ones you built yourself in the first eighteen parts
cena: Nine at night, third in at the bar with your elbow on the zinc: the man next to you orders, the woman behind the bar answers, and neither sentence has an S left in it — and none of it is for you.
frasePiso: If all you take from this part is that the S can vanish, you will still follow more of a Spanish bar than most people who spend a fortnight in one.
permissao: You are allowed to catch one word in five and keep listening: take that word, use it, and let the rest go past. You never correct anybody — plenty of Spain says 'grasias' rather than 'grathias', and nobody there is wrong. And you will never have to talk like this yourself. Understanding it is the whole job.
espelho: Leaving a clean gap at the end of your sentence is the bit that reads as odd there. There was no gap at all in what you just heard, and that is not rudeness — a pause that size is read as you having finished with the subject, and somebody else takes it.

fichasCulturais.sinal: The barman says a sentence to you that you follow, then turns to the man beside you and says the next one at twice the speed.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: I understood him a second ago and now I understand nothing — my Spanish only works when somebody is being kind to me.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: Speech aimed at a visitor is slowed and fully pronounced; speech aimed at the regular next to him is not. What changed in that second was the audience, not the language.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Stay in it. Count the beats instead of hunting for the letters, and keep the one word you did catch.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: You keep listening through the fast half of the room instead of switching off at the first sentence that is not for you — and the fast half is where the recommendation gets made.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not at a hotel desk or a ticket window, where the whole exchange runs at visitor speed all day and there is no faster version underneath it.

fichasCulturais.sinal: A word you know well arrives with a hole in the middle of it — pescado comes out as pescao — and nobody repeats it.
fichasCulturais.suaLeitura: That was a dish I have never heard of, so I will point at something else on the list.
fichasCulturais.oQueEAli: The D between two vowels drops out in ordinary relaxed speech across Spain, not only in one corner of it. The word was not swapped for another one; it was worn down.
fichasCulturais.oQueVoceFaz: Put the D back in your head and take the order. Say the dish back with the D in if you want to check — you are understood either way.
fichasCulturais.oQueMelhora: You eat the fish the house is proud of instead of the safe thing you could already pronounce.
fichasCulturais.ondeNaoVale: Not on a written menu, where the D is always in place — this one is a hearing problem, and it disappears the moment anything is on paper.

fatosDatados.afirmacao: Most of peninsular Spain distinguishes the 'th' of gracias from a plain S; seseo — everything as a plain S — is standard in the Canaries, in parts of Andalusia and across the Americas.
fatosDatados.fonte: RAE/ASALE, Diccionario panhispánico de dudas, verbetes «seseo» e «ceceo»

fatosDatados.afirmacao: At the end of a syllable the S is aspirated or dropped, and the D between two vowels falls out in ordinary relaxed speech — the second one across Spain, not only in the south.

aprofundar.titulo: What the ear module trains, and why nobody speaks in it (optional reading)

secoes.titulo: Why there is no speaking in this one
secoes.corpo: Your brain recognises far more than it can produce, and the gap between the two is the cheapest thing in the whole course to close. You already own the sentences; what you do not own yet is the ability to spot them when a third of the sounds have gone. So this part spends its twelve minutes entirely on the receiving side, and it is the only part of the course where you are asked to say nothing at all. That is deliberate and it is not a day off: recognising a worn-down sentence is a different skill from producing a careful one, and the only way to build it is exposure to the worn-down version of things you already know. This is also why every single sentence in here came out of an earlier part. A new sentence would have made it a vocabulary lesson with a difficult accent on top, and you would have learned neither. And to be plain about the ambition: you will never need to speak like this. You will absolutely need to understand it, because it starts exactly where the hotel English stops.

exemplos.es: ¿Me pones dos cañas, por favor? → ¿Me poneh doh cañah, por favó?
exemplos.pt: the same order twice — the second one is the one you will actually be standing next to

exemplos.es: El pescado está muy bueno. → El pescao está mu bueno.
exemplos.pt: the fish is very good — same fish, same price, one letter shorter

secoes.titulo: The four things that happen to fast Spanish, in the order you meet them
secoes.corpo: One: the S at the end of a syllable turns into a soft puff of air and then into nothing, so dos cervezas comes out closer to 'doh thervetha'. Two: the 'th' of gracias and cerveza is a plain S in some places — that is seseo, and the RAE and ASALE describe it as standard in the Canaries, in parts of Andalusia and throughout the Americas, with the 'th' distinction holding across most of the rest of peninsular Spain. Three: the D between two vowels drops out, so pescado becomes pescao, cansado becomes cansao, pagado becomes pagao — and this one is ordinary relaxed speech all over Spain, not a southern thing. Four: the R and the L at the end of a word soften, so pagar becomes pagá and para llevar becomes pa' llevá. Item two has a primary source behind it; items one, three and four are the settled description you will find in any dialectology of Spanish, but we have not put a single primary citation next to them, and this is us saying so rather than dressing it up. Nothing in the audio depends on the difference: what the audio asks of you is to recognise your own sentences with holes in them, and holes are holes whoever put them there.

exemplos.pt: it is already paid — two holes in four words, and it still settles the bill

exemplos.es: Para llevar, por favor. → Pa' llevá, por favó.
exemplos.pt: to take away, please — the R on the end going, twice in one breath

secoes.titulo: Two different people, not two accents — and why we are being careful about that
secoes.corpo: The careful recordings in this part are the same voices you have been learning from since part one. The fast recordings are two other people, and that is the honest description of what changed: another person, another rhythm, another speed, the same Spanish. We are deliberately not telling you that the second voice is from Seville, or from anywhere else, because we have not verified that it is, and a course that tells you what a region sounds like on the strength of a recording it did not check is teaching you an accent that may not exist. The distinction matters for a practical reason too. If you file this away as 'southern Spanish', you will switch the skill off the moment you are in the north — and the fast version is what you get at a busy counter in any city in the country, at nine at night, from somebody who has four orders in his head. The rule that survives all of it is the one the hand has been teaching you since part one: the number of beats does not change. Count those and you will find the sentence even when half the consonants have gone.

exemplos.pt: anything else? — five beats either way, three fewer letters
where are the toilets? — the front of están goes as well as the ends

secoes.titulo: The one thing you should never do with any of this
secoes.corpo: Never correct anybody. If somebody says 'grasias' where you were taught 'grathias', they are speaking their own language in their own way and there is nothing to fix. The same goes for the dropped S and the missing D: they are not sloppiness and they are not an error, any more than a Londoner saying 'wa'er' has misspelled water. Correcting a native speaker's own pronunciation is the single fastest way to turn a friendly counter into a cold one, and it is a mistake almost exclusively made by people who have just finished a language course. The useful reflex in the other direction is the one from part three: when you genuinely have not got it, you do not ask for it again — again gets you the same speed, one notch louder — you ask for it slower, by name. And when even that fails, take the one word you did catch, use it, and let the rest go. Understanding four words in five is not a partial result at a bar. It is how everybody there is listening, including them.

exemplos.es: ¿Me puede hablar más despacio, por favor?
exemplos.pt: could you speak more slowly, please — asks for speed, not for repetition
👂 sorry? — what you will hear them use on each other, and it gets the sentence back at the same speed
